sources.news_title: Trump Signs Deal with Greenland
sources.text:
President Trump signed a deal with the leaders of Greenland and Denmark that allows the United States to form a stronger military presence in the region.
“President Donald J. Trump officially signs the landmark Greenland security deal alongside Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of Denmark and Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen of Greenland,” the White House posted on X, sharing a video of the signing. “This HISTORIC deal is critical for American national security and defense in the Arctic Region.”
President Trump addressed the deal in his speech before the United Nations General Assembly. “No U.S. adversary will ever be permitted to establish a military presence in Greenland anymore, or make sensitive investments there without our express written approval,” he said. “We will immediately begin the process of developing a large military presence in the appropriate locations.”
The text of the agreement, also shared by the White House, explains that the “security situation in the Arctic is changing and that more efforts are needed to ensure security there in the future.” The agreement goes on to state that the United States is permitted to “modernize and expand its activities in Pituffik Space Base,” as well as “establish an additional Defense Area at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig in accordance with modalities and technical details to be mutually agreed by the Parties.”
The United States may also “enjoy, for its public vessels and aircraft and its armed forces and vehicles, the right of free access to and movement between the Defense Areas through Greenland, including the Territorial Waters, by land, air and sea,” it says. It may also “fly over and land in any territory in Greenland, including the Territorial Waters, and United States public vessels may have undersea access to and movement within the Territorial Waters, without restriction except as mutually agreed upon by the Parties.”
Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen previously expressed optimism on the arrangement. “A period of uncertainty will hopefully be replaced by a binding agreement that strengthens security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic — and thus also our shared security within NATO and Europe — while respecting the Kingdom’s red lines,” he wrote on Instagram.
Similarly, Greenland’s prime minister, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, acknowledged that the agreement “recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of our kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination.”

US PRESIDENT DONALD Trump has signed a security deal with the leaders of Greenland and Denmark.
“It’s going to be a long-term, fantastic relationship,” Trump said at a signing ceremony on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.
“This is tremendous for Europe and for the United States and for everybody,” he added.
Under the 10-page pact, the United States will build two military bases in southern and eastern Greenland.
These will be established in Narsarsuaq in the south of the island and Mestersvig in the east, in addition to the Pituffik base it already operates in the north.
The deal also reaffirmed “the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark” while recognising Greenland’s “right to self-determination.”
Since returning to the presidency in January 2025, Trump repeatedly insisted that the United States needed to control Greenland for strategic reasons, alarming NATO ally Denmark and sparking fierce pushback from the alliance.
When announcing the deal on Friday, Trump said the arrangement would give America “permanent control” over security for the territory.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said her country “stands in a better place than we did yesterday” with the agreement.
“As everyone knows, we live in uncertain times,” she told reporters after signing the deal.
“I hope the agreement will bring more peace of mind in Greenland, because it has been a tough time,” she said.
Earlier, she told Trump that his message has been clear: “You don’t want adversaries to come too close.”
“I fully agree, and with this deal, they are not,” she added.
Greenland’s prime minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen added that Greenland matters for North American security and for transatlantic security.
“This agreement reflects that we understand our responsibility and act accordingly,” he added.
He later said that while the pact is a step in a good direction, “back home we need to rebuild trust, and that will be a process for us.”
The agreement blocks non-NATO, non-EU countries from strategic sectors in Greenland, in an attempt to bar US adversaries China and Russia from gaining a foothold in the Arctic.
Such parties will generally not be allowed “control, significant influence, or access to non-public information that may constitute a threat to national security or public order” within sensitive sectors.
EU chief Antonio Costa welcomed the deal on Tuesday as a “positive step for transatlantic cooperation and Arctic security.”
“The EU stands ready to continue working closely with Greenland, Denmark and our transatlantic partners for a peaceful, secure and prosperous Arctic,” Costa posted on X.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz similarly expressed support for the deal.
The agreement also stipulates that Greenland, home to 57,000 inhabitants, must continue to abide by the agreement even if it obtains independence from Denmark.
It should also remain in or join NATO “if necessary.”
Under a 1951 defence pact updated in 2004, Washington was already able to ramp up its military presence on the island provided it informed Denmark and Greenland in advance.

sources.news_title: EXPLAINER: What is in the US-Greenland-Denmark security deal?
What is in the US-Greenland-Denmark security deal?
sources.text:
The United States, Denmark and Greenland have signed a security agreement aimed at ending months of tension over the Danish self-governing territory after US President Donald Trump's repeated threats to take control of the vast Arctic island.
Here are some key components of the deal, which adds to a 1951 US-Danish pact on Greenland's defence, according to a text published by the Danish government.
What are the military aspects of the deal?
The agreement allows the United States to establish two new military bases - one at Narsarsuaq in southern Greenland and the other at Mestersvig on the east coast - and to expand Pituffik Space Base, currently its only active base on the island.
US craft including planes and vessels get flyover, landing and undersea rights in all of Greenland, including territorial waters.
The agreement does not specify troop numbers or timelines.
How does the pact work with NATO?
The agreement expresses support for a stronger NATO presence in the Arctic, and Denmark commits to further strengthen its own security posture in the region.
If Greenland ever become independent, Denmark and Greenland must ensure the new state remains in NATO, applying for membership if necessary.
Non-NATO members are barred from having an ongoing military presence in Greenland.
What rights does Greenland have?
The agreement says it respects Greenland's right to self-determination.
Under the accord, the US must act in a way that respects Greenlandic society and the Greenlandic way of life.
What are the economic aspects of the pact?
The agreement does not address US interests or investments into Greenland's mining and resources sector.
The deal bars investors from outside NATO member states, NATO partners or the European Union from having control or major influence over sensitive sectors in Greenland.
Greenland will screen investments to enforce those rules.
What happens now?
The parliaments of Greenland and Denmark must approve the agreement before it goes into effect.
The pact has no end date and can be amended only by mutual consent.

Trump signs Greenland security deal with Denmark and Greenland
sources.text:
United Nations President Donald Trump has signed an agreement with Denmark and Greenland aimed at strengthening Arctic and North Atlantic security, easing tensions over his repeated calls for Greenland to become part of the United States.
The signing Tuesday on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York comes days after Trump announced the deal to bolster US military presence on the vast, icy island but keep it under Danish control. The governments provided few details of the agreement before the signing.
“This is tremendous for Europe and for the United States and for everybody,” Trump said just before the agreement was signed. “And for Greenland, it's going to be incredible.”
For months, Trump has expressed his desire for Greenland to become part of the United States and issued threats to seize the semiautonomous territory from Denmark, a NATO ally. On Tuesday, he did not respond to questions about whether a US acquisition of Greenland was off the table.
The US has had a presence in Greenland for many years
Officials from the US, Greenland and Denmark negotiated for months behind the scenes, searching for solutions to address some of Trump's security concerns about the mineral-rich island.
Trump's designs on Greenland strained relations within NATO, with Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen warning a US takeover would amount to the end of the Atlantic alliance.
The standoff unsettled many of Greenland's roughly 56,000 people and drove a wedge between the US and Denmark and its European Union partners, who stepped up security exercises on and monetary support for the island.
Trade and hopes for a resource grab have all factored into concerns about Greenland's future: About two-thirds of its territory sits inside the Arctic Circle, where melting sea ice has opened additional shipping routes
The United States was prominent in Greenland for decades but, since 1945, the US military presence in Greenland has decreased from thousands of soldiers on 17 bases and installations to roughly 200 soldiers on the remote Pituffik Space Base in the northwest. The base supports missile warning, missile defense and space surveillance operations for the US and NATO.
Addressing the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday morning, Trump provided a small window into details of the deal.
“We will immediately begin the process of developing a large military presence in the appropriate locations,” he said, including “building two very major military bases.”
Denmark's parliament approved a bill last year to allow US military bases on Danish soil, widening a 2023 military agreement made with the Biden administration that gave US troops broad access to air bases in Denmark.
Trump previously insisted the US needed to “take Greenland,” to prevent Russia or China from doing the same. Though Trump said he would rather “ make a deal ” for the territory, he added: “one way or the other, we're going to have Greenland.”
All parties present the agreement as a positive move
Mikkel Runge Olesen, a senior researcher at the Danish Institute of International Studies, said Greenland and Denmark come away from the deal with the possibility of “ending the crisis without compromising on sovereignty,” while the US gets a “somewhat more favourable” deal than under the existing defense treaty.
But relations overall between the US, Denmark and Greenland “are likely to be haunted by this long after Trump leaves office, and the crisis is likely to have significant and lasting negative impact on transatlantic relations more generally,” he said. “The lost trust will take decades to rebuild.”
Frederiksen said Tuesday that the deal being signed was a “deal that can last forever,” labelling it as good for the US, Greenland, Denmark and the broader NATO alliance.
“Mr President, you have been very clear: You don't want adversaries to come too close,” she said. “I fully agree.”
Jens-Frederik Nielsen, Greenland's prime minister, called it “a win-win-win agreement.”
“Your security is our security, and our security is your security,” he said Tuesday.

sources.news_title: Trump Claims ‘Permanent Control’ Over Greenland Security Deal
sources.text:
President Donald Trump has secured what he describes as a “permanent” US security foothold in Greenland under a new agreement allowing Washington to establish additional military bases across the strategically important Arctic island.
The arrangement expands on the existing US presence at Pituffik Space Base, a key installation supporting American missile-warning and space surveillance systems. It would permit the Pentagon to develop further sites across Greenland’s remote and unforgiving terrain.
Signed Tuesday with Danish officials, the agreement also prevents other countries—particularly Russia and China—from setting up military bases on Greenland. Both nations have sought to strengthen their position and influence in the Arctic.
For Trump, the deal represents a compromise after years of openly advocating US ownership of Greenland. He has previously floated buying the island, annexing it or even using military force to bring it under American control.
Greenland is a semi-autonomous territory within the Kingdom of Denmark and occupies a pivotal position in US defense planning. Its location in the North Atlantic places it near a crucial Arctic passage where Russian and Chinese vessels have been increasingly observed.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen joined Trump at the signing ceremony.
“So this is tremendous for Europe and for the United States, for everybody, and for Greenland,” Trump said, describing the agreement as the foundation of a “long-term, fantastic relationship.”
Nielsen underscored the shared security commitment, telling Trump after the signing: “Our security is your security.”
President Donald Trump marked the new Greenland-Denmark security agreement during a signing ceremony held alongside the UN General Assembly meeting Tuesday
The agreement gives the US authority to develop additional military installations in Greenland, strengthening the Pentagon’s Arctic presence
New US installations under the agreement would provide NATO with a stronger platform for monitoring and responding to activity across the Arctic.
Trump first revealed the agreement in a social media post last week.
At the time, he said the deal granted the United States “permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland,” claiming it addressed “ALL of our many US concerns.”
“At my direction, we worked with representatives of Denmark and Greenland to guarantee that the United States will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the security of Greenland and the United States of America,” Trump wrote. He characterized the arrangement as an agreement with an “infinite life.”
Trump also asserted that no US adversary would be able to establish a base, maintain a military presence or make sensitive investments in Greenland without Washington’s explicit written approval.
However, the agreement stops short of transferring sovereignty over Greenland to the United States, despite Trump’s past threats to seize the territory.
“No, I never take military force off the table,” Trump told NBC News in a 2025 interview when asked about acquiring the island. “But I think there’s a good possibility that we could do it without military force.”
Trump has presented his campaign to acquire Greenland as a matter of national security, pointing to the island’s Arctic location and the efforts by China and Russia to expand their regional military and commercial reach.
General Gregory M. Guillot, who leads US Northern Command, has said Greenland could host part of a wider Arctic radar network linking American installations in Alaska and Canada.
He has also said the United States is interested in developing a deepwater port and a base for US special operations forces on the island.
Trump first floated the idea of bringing Greenland into the US sphere of influence during his first term in 2019.

Trade and hopes for a resource grab have all factored into concerns about Greenland’s future: About two-thirds of its territory sits inside the Arctic Circle, where melting sea ice has opened additional shipping routes.
The United States was prominent in Greenland for decades but, since 1945, the U.S. military presence in Greenland has decreased from thousands of soldiers on 17 bases and installations to roughly 200 soldiers on the remote Pituffik Space Base in the northwest. The base supports missile warning, missile defense and space surveillance operations for the U.S. and NATO.
Addressing the United Nations General Assembly ahead of the signing, Trump said the U.S. would “immediately begin the process of developing a large military presence in the appropriate locations,” including “building two very major military bases.”
Denmark’s parliament approved a bill last year to allow U.S. military bases on Danish soil, widening a 2023 agreement made with the Biden administration that gave U.S. troops broad access to air bases in Denmark.
Trump previously insisted the U.S. needed to “take Greenland,” to prevent Russia or China from doing the same. Though Trump said he would rather “ make a deal ” for the territory, he added: “one way or the other, we’re going to have Greenland.”
The agreement, released by the Greenlandic, Danish, American governments after the signing, allows for Washington to “modernize and expand” its activities at Pituffik.
It also says the U.S. can set up “defense areas” at Narsarsuaq in the south and Mestersvig in the east, and that it “may establish additional defense areas in Greenland and strengthen its military operations or facilities.” Washington is to award contracts for goods and services related to setting up, maintaining or dismantling such bases “to Greenlandic sources to the maximum extent possible.”
The accord calls for wide U.S. military mobility on Greenland’s territory, including “undersea access.”
No non-NATO country will be allowed to set up “its own manned or unmanned military installations in Greenland,” or to have a “persistent” military presence unless the signatories agree otherwise.
The accord “does not have an end date,” and if Greenland chooses to become independent, it will agree to remain in NATO and take on Denmark’s rights and obligations under the deal.
All parties present the agreement as a positive move.
Frederiksen said Tuesday called the agreement a “deal that can last forever,” labeling it as good for the U.S., Greenland, Denmark and the broader NATO alliance.
“Mr. President, you have been very clear: You don’t want adversaries to come too close,” she said. “I fully agree.”
Jens-Frederik Nielsen, Greenland’s prime minister, called it “a win-win-win agreement.”
“Your security is our security,” he said, “and our security is your security.”
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte, who helped turn down the temperature at the height of the crisis in January, celebrated the accord’s signing, writing on X that “this agreement, along with NATO’s growing role in securing this vital region, enhances our collective security and supports a safer and more stable future for us all.”
But the standoff won’t be forgotten quickly.
“A lot of trust has been tested, I would say,” Naaja Nathanielsen, one of Greenland’s two lawmakers in the Danish parliament and a former government minister in Nuuk, told The Associated Press. “It’s been really difficult in Greenland and people have been generally afraid and worried about everything, from losing our country, to our livelihoods and so on.”
Nevertheless, Nathanielsen called the accord “a huge step in the right direction,” and praised it as the first binding agreement Greenland has signed as a country.
“For us, that is a huge step forward in our quest for more self autonomy and a bigger seat at the table,” she said.

President Donald Trump joined the leaders of Denmark and Greenland in signing a new Arctic security agreement Tuesday that will expand U.S. military operations on Greenland while leaving sovereignty over the semiautonomous territory unchanged.
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom.
President Donald Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen signed a trilateral security agreement Tuesday that will substantially expand the U.S. military presence in Greenland while keeping the Arctic territory within the Kingdom of Denmark.
The agreement was signed on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York after months of negotiations prompted in part by Trump’s repeated calls for greater American control over Greenland.
WATCH:
“This is tremendous for Europe and for the United States and for everybody,” Trump said before the signing. “And for Greenland, it’s going to be incredible.”
The agreement strengthens U.S. access to Greenland for defense operations and is intended to bolster security in the Arctic and North Atlantic, according to Denmark’s government and reporting from The Associated Press and Reuters. It does not transfer sovereignty over Greenland to the United States.
Frederiksen said the agreement protects the political status of Greenland while strengthening security cooperation among NATO allies.
“Mr. President, you have been very clear: You don’t want adversaries to come too close,” Frederiksen said. “I fully agree.”
She described the agreement as a “deal that can last forever” and said it benefits the United States, Denmark, Greenland and NATO.
Nielsen offered a similar assessment.
“Your security is our security, and our security is your security,” he said, calling the pact “a win-win-win agreement.”
Denmark had previously said the agreement recognizes “the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the Greenlandic people’s right to self-determination.”
The signing marked a change from the confrontation that dominated U.S.-Danish relations over Greenland for much of Trump’s second term.
Trump had repeatedly said the United States needed Greenland for national security and had suggested that Washington should acquire the territory before Russia or China increased their strategic presence in the Arctic.
His comments alarmed Danish and Greenlandic officials and generated concerns within NATO about tensions between alliance members.
The new agreement instead expands U.S. defense access without making Greenland American territory.
Trump did not answer reporters Tuesday when asked whether the possibility of the United States eventually acquiring Greenland was now permanently off the table.
Two New U.S. Military Locations Planned
Trump provided additional information about the pact during his Tuesday address to the U.N. General Assembly.
“We will immediately begin the process of developing a large military presence in the appropriate locations,” Trump said, including “building two very major military bases.”
Reuters reported that the agreement provides for a renewed U.S. presence at Narsarsuaq in southern Greenland and another military location at Mestersvig on the east coast.
Narsarsuaq was previously used by the United States during the Cold War, while Mestersvig is currently associated with Denmark’s Sirius Dog Sled Patrol and other government operations.
The United States already operates Pituffik Space Base in northwestern Greenland.
Pituffik supports missile warning, missile defense and space surveillance operations for the United States and NATO.
The planned expansion would represent the most significant increase in permanent or semi-permanent U.S. military infrastructure on Greenland since the Cold War.
At the height of America’s Cold War presence, the United States operated 17 bases and installations on the island and stationed thousands of military personnel there.
That footprint steadily declined after the Soviet Union collapsed.
Today, roughly 200 U.S. military personnel are stationed at Pituffik, according to AP.
Agreement Emerged After Months of Tension
Trump’s pursuit of Greenland had strained relations with Denmark, which is both a NATO member and a longstanding U.S. ally.
He repeatedly argued that control of the island was necessary to prevent Russian or Chinese strategic expansion in the Arctic.
Though Trump sometimes said he preferred to acquire Greenland through negotiation, he also said earlier this year that “one way or the other, we’re going to have Greenland.”
Frederiksen repeatedly rejected the possibility of transferring sovereignty.
She warned that any attempt by one NATO country to seize territory from another would threaten the foundations of the alliance.
The political confrontation also caused concern among Greenland’s roughly 56,000 residents.
Greenland is largely self-governing but remains constitutionally part of the Kingdom of Denmark. Copenhagen retains responsibility for foreign affairs and defense, though Greenland has progressively gained greater authority over domestic matters.
The island’s strategic importance has grown as Arctic temperatures rise, sea ice retreats and new maritime routes become increasingly accessible.
Approximately two-thirds of Greenland lies within the Arctic Circle.
The island also contains significant deposits of critical minerals and rare earth elements, adding an economic dimension to the geopolitical competition surrounding it.
Officials from all three governments spent months working on a formula that could address Trump’s security concerns without transferring Greenlandic sovereignty.
Tuesday’s agreement appears to represent that compromise.
Reuters reported that the pact expands U.S. military access, includes provisions aimed at keeping hostile non-NATO powers from establishing military footholds in Greenland and updates the security framework built around the longstanding U.S.-Danish defense relationship.
Pact Builds on Decades-Old Defense Agreement
American military access to Greenland dates back decades.
The United States and Denmark signed a defense agreement in 1951 during the early Cold War, giving Washington broad rights to operate military facilities on the island.
That agreement was amended in 2004 as Greenland gained greater political autonomy.
The new security arrangement updates that framework while expanding American access to additional areas, according to Reuters.
Denmark’s government had said before Tuesday’s ceremony that the agreement would not formally enter into force until required national parliamentary procedures were completed.
The arrangement also places Greenland’s defense more clearly within a wider NATO strategy for the Arctic and North Atlantic.
Denmark has argued that Arctic security should be treated as a collective alliance responsibility rather than solely a U.S.-Greenland matter.
Russian military expansion across its Arctic territory and growing Chinese economic and scientific activity in the region have increased NATO’s focus on the far north.
Denmark Also Expanded U.S. Access at Home
The Greenland agreement follows another expansion of American military access within the Kingdom of Denmark.
Denmark’s parliament previously approved legislation implementing a defense cooperation agreement that gives U.S. forces broader access to designated military facilities in Denmark itself.
That arrangement originated in a 2023 agreement negotiated during the Biden administration.
Together, the Denmark and Greenland arrangements give the U.S. military greater flexibility across the North Atlantic and Arctic approaches to North America and Europe.
For Washington, Greenland is particularly important because of its location between the continental United States, Russia and Europe.
Early-warning radars and space-surveillance systems based there can detect missile launches and monitor satellites and other objects passing across polar trajectories.
Analysts Say Deal Resolves Sovereignty Dispute Without Ending Strategic Tension
Mikkel Runge Olesen, a senior researcher at the Danish Institute of International Studies, said the agreement allows Copenhagen and Nuuk to resolve the immediate crisis without surrendering Greenland.
He said Denmark and Greenland gained the possibility of “ending the crisis without compromising on sovereignty,” while the United States secured a “somewhat more favorable” security arrangement than it had under the existing defense framework.
Olesen cautioned that the political damage from the dispute may last beyond the agreement.
Relations between the United States, Denmark and Greenland “are likely to be haunted by this long after Trump leaves office, and the crisis is likely to have significant and lasting negative impact on transatlantic relations more generally,” he said.
“The lost trust will take decades to rebuild.”
That assessment is one analyst’s view rather than an official position of any of the three governments.
The leaders signing the agreement instead emphasized cooperation.
Frederiksen said it would strengthen the security of NATO and Europe while respecting Danish sovereignty and Greenlandic self-determination.
Nielsen presented the agreement as evidence that Greenland could strengthen its security relationship with Washington without changing its political status.
Trump described the agreement as a major security achievement for both sides of the Atlantic.
The pact therefore closes at least one chapter in a dispute that had raised the possibility of a deeper split between Washington and Copenhagen.
The United States will gain a much larger military footprint in Greenland, including two additional major facilities, while Denmark and Greenland retain sovereignty over the island.
What remains unresolved is whether Tuesday’s agreement ends Trump’s broader interest in U.S. ownership of Greenland.
Asked directly whether acquisition was now off the table, Trump did not answer.
For the moment, however, the three governments have replaced the argument over ownership with a defense arrangement that greatly expands America’s ability to operate militarily from one of the world’s most strategically important Arctic territories.

US to build 2 military bases in southern and eastern Greenland
Summary
The United States, Greenland and Denmark signed a security agreement on Tuesday in New York that will let Washington build two military bases in southern and eastern Greenland. The deal also reaffirms Denmark’s sovereignty and Greenland’s right to self-determination, while giving the U.S. control over security in the autonomous Arctic territory. It bars non-NATO and non-EU countries from strategic sectors in Greenland and requires Greenland to stay in or join NATO if needed. The agreement comes as Trump has pushed for U.S. control of Greenland for strategic reasons.
Key Facts
- The new U.S. bases will be located in Narsarsuaq in southern Greenland and Mestersvig in eastern Greenland.
- The U.S. already operates the Pituffik base in northern Greenland.
- The agreement was signed on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.
- It says states or investors from countries outside NATO, NATO partners and the EU cannot have control, significant influence or access to non-public information in particularly sensitive Greenland sectors unless the parties agree it poses no security threat.
- Greenland, which has 57,000 inhabitants, must continue to abide by the agreement even if it gains independence from Denmark.
COPENHAGEN — The United States will build two military bases in southern and eastern Greenland under a wide-ranging security agreement signed Tuesday between the United States, Greenland and Denmark on Tuesday.
Since returning to the White House in January 2025, Trump has repeatedly insisted that the U.S. needed to control Greenland for strategic reasons, alarming NATO ally Denmark and sparking fierce pushback from the alliance.
On Tuesday, Washington, Copenhagen and Nuuk signed a 10-page agreement in New York, on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, giving the U.S. control over security in Denmark's autonomous Arctic territory.
Under the deal — which reaffirmed "the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark" and recognised Greenland's "right to self-determination" — Washington will establish military bases in Narsarsuaq in the south of the island and Mestersvig in the east, in addition to the Pituffik base it already operates in the north.
In a section aimed at barring U.S. adversaries China and Russia from gaining a foothold in the Arctic, the agreement blocks non-NATO, non-EU countries from strategic sectors in Greenland.
"The Parties agree that states or investors from a state that is not a member of NATO, a NATO partner, or an EU member state shall not be allowed to have control, significant influence, or access to non-public information that may constitute a threat to national security or public order within particularly sensitive sectors or activities in the territory of Greenland (including the Territorial Waters), unless agreed between the Parties that the activities of such states or investors would not constitute a threat to national security or public order," the agreement says.
The agreement also stipulates that Greenland, home to 57,000 inhabitants, must continue to abide by the agreement even if it obtains independence from Denmark, and must remain in or join NATO "if necessary".
Under a 1951 defence pact updated in 2004, Washington was already able to ramp up its military presence on the island provided it informed Denmark and Greenland in advance.

sources.text:
The United States will be allowed to establish military bases at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig and expand its activities at Pituffik Space Base under a new security agreement signed by US President Donald Trump, Denmark and Greenland on Tuesday (September 22).
The agreement, signed on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, strengthens US military access to Greenland while keeping the territory under Danish control.
The pact also sets out security conditions for any future independence of Greenland, including a requirement that an independent Greenland remain part of NATO.
“It's going to be a long-term, fantastic relationship,” Trump said at the signing ceremony.
Trump said the agreement would give the United States “permanent control over security and all other needs” in Greenland.
“No US adversary will ever be permitted to establish a military presence in Greenland any more, or make sensitive investments there without our express written approval,” Trump said in his UN speech before the signing.
Here is what the US-Denmark-Greenland agreement means:
Under the agreement, the United States will be allowed to establish military bases at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig.
Washington will also be permitted to modernise and expand its activities at Pituffik Space Base, the US military installation in northwestern Greenland.
The agreement allows US aircraft to fly over and land in any territory in Greenland, including its territorial waters.
Trump had earlier said the US would begin developing a “large military presence” in Greenland, including “building two very major military bases.”
The agreement also allows the United States to establish its Golden Dome defence system in Greenland.
The provision would give Washington an expanded role in the island's air and missile defence architecture, amid growing US concerns about security in the Arctic and North Atlantic.
The pact also says that no state that is not a NATO member will be allowed to establish its own manned or unmanned military installations in Greenland.
A major provision of the agreement deals with Greenland's possible future independence.
If Greenland exercises its right to become independent, Denmark and Greenland must work together to ensure that the independent Greenlandic state agrees to remain in NATO, including by applying to become a member of the alliance.
The independent state would also be expected to honour the defence agreement.
The provision links Greenland's future security arrangements to the NATO alliance even if its constitutional relationship with Denmark changes.
The agreement also introduces restrictions on foreign investment in sensitive sectors.
Investors from countries outside NATO and the European Union will be barred from certain sensitive sectors in Greenland, with the agreement citing potential security threats.
The parties also agree to work together to counter espionage in Greenland.
Despite the expanded US military role, the agreement places conditions on how Washington exercises its access rights.
It states that US access must be exercised in a manner that respects Greenlandic society and the Greenlandic way of life.
Denmark will also continue to strengthen its own security posture in the Arctic.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte welcomed the agreement, saying it would enhance collective security.
The agreement, he said, supports “a safer and more stable future for us all.”
The pact places NATO at the centre of the security framework for Greenland and the wider Arctic region.
The agreement comes after months of tension over Trump's repeated calls for the United States to acquire Greenland.
Trump had argued that US control of Greenland was necessary to prevent Russia or China from gaining a stronger foothold in the Arctic. His demands strained relations with Denmark, a NATO ally, and triggered a wider diplomatic dispute within the alliance.
The new agreement does not transfer Greenland to the United States. Instead, it expands Washington's military access and security role while leaving the territory under Danish sovereignty.
The agreement is subject to the necessary parliamentary procedures in the Kingdom of Denmark together with Greenland.
Its provisions therefore still face the required domestic approval processes before they can take full effect.

sources.news_title: Trump signs U.S.-Denmark-Greenland agreement to bolster Arctic security
sources.text: UNITED NATIONS — U.S. President Donald Trump on Tuesday signed an agreement with Denmark and Greenland aimed at strengthening Arctic and North Atlantic security, paving the way for more U.S. bases in Greenland and easing tensions over his repeated calls for the vast island to become part of the United States. The signing on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York comes days after Trump announced the deal to bolster the U.S. military presence on Greenland but keep it under Danish control. The agreement would still apply if Greenland eventually chooses independence. “This is tremendous for Europe and for the United States and for everybody,” Trump said just before the agreement was signed. “And for Greenland, it’s going to be incredible.” Trump has expressed his desire to acquire Greenland since as long ago as 2019 and, during his second term, issued threats to seize the semiautonomous territory from Denmark, a NATO ally. On Tuesday, he did not respond to questions about whether a U.S. acquisition of Greenland was off the table. The U.S. has had a presence in Greenland for decades Officials from the U.S., Greenland and Denmark negotiated for months behind the scenes, searching for solutions to address some of Trump’s security concerns about the mineral-rich island. Trump’s designs on Greenland strained relations within NATO, with Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen warning a U.S. takeover would amount to the end of the Atlantic alliance. The standoff unsettled many of Greenland’s roughly 56,000 people and drove a wedge between the U.S. and Denmark and its European Union partners, who stepped up security exercises on and monetary support for the island. Trade and hopes for a resource grab have factored into concerns about Greenland’s future. About two-thirds of its territory sits inside the Arctic Circle, where melting sea ice has opened additional shipping routes. The United States was prominent in Greenland for decades but, since 1945, the U.S. military presence in Greenland has decreased from thousands of soldiers on 17 bases and installations to roughly 200 soldiers on the remote Pituffik Space Base in the northwest. The base supports missile warning, missile defence and space surveillance operations for the U.S. and NATO. Addressing the United Nations General Assembly ahead of the signing, Trump said the U.S. would “immediately begin the process of developing a large military presence in the appropriate locations,” including “building two very major military bases.” Denmark’s parliament approved a bill last year to allow U.S. military bases on Danish soil, widening a 2023 agreement made with the Biden administration that gave U.S. troops broad access to air bases in Denmark. Trump previously insisted the U.S. needed to “take Greenland,” to prevent Russia or China from doing the same. Though Trump said he would rather " make a deal " for the territory, he added, “one way or the other, we’re going to have Greenland.” The accord will remain in effect if Greenland becomes independent The agreement, released by all three governments after the signing, allows for Washington to “modernize and expand” its activities at Pituffik. It also says the U.S. can set up “defence areas” at Narsarsuaq in the south and Mestersvig in the east, and that it “may establish additional defence areas in Greenland and strengthen its military operations or facilities.” Washington is to award contracts for goods and services related to setting up, maintaining or dismantling such bases “to Greenlandic sources to the maximum extent possible.” The accord calls for wide U.S. military mobility on Greenland’s territory, including “undersea access.” It says the signatories share an interest in allowing the U.S. military access to Greenland to defend the NATO area, Greenland itself and the American continent -- including through “Golden Dome,” Trump’s planned missile defence system. Frederiksen said no decision had been made on the specifics of that system. No non-NATO country will be allowed to set up “its own manned or unmanned military installations in Greenland,” or to have a “persistent” military presence unless the signatories agree otherwise. The accord “does not have an end date” and, if Greenland chooses to become independent, it will agree to remain in NATO and take on Denmark’s rights and obligations under the deal. All parties present the agreement as a positive move Frederiksen on Tuesday called the agreement a “deal that can last forever,” labelling it as good for the U.S., Greenland, Denmark and the broader NATO alliance. “Mr. President, you have been very clear: You don’t want adversaries to come too close,” she said. “I fully agree.” Jens-Frederik Nielsen, Greenland’s prime minister, called it “a win-win-win agreement.” “Your security is our security,” he said, “and our security is your security.” NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte, who helped turn down the temperature at the height of the crisis in January, celebrated the accord’s signing, writing on X that “this agreement, along with NATO’s growing role in securing this vital region, enhances our collective security and supports a safer and more stable future for us all.” But the standoff won’t be forgotten quickly. “A lot of trust has been tested, I would say,” Naaja Nathanielsen, one of Greenland’s two lawmakers in the Danish parliament and a former government minister in Nuuk, told The Associated Press. “It’s been really difficult in Greenland and people have been generally afraid and worried about everything, from losing our country to our livelihoods and so on.” Nevertheless, Nathanielsen called the accord “a huge step in the right direction,” and praised it as the first binding agreement Greenland has signed as a country. “For us, that is a huge step forward in our quest for more self-autonomy and a bigger seat at the table,” she said. A clearly relieved Frederiksen said at a post-signing appearance with Nielsen that “the kingdom of Denmark is in a better place than we were yesterday.” She concluded the news conference by saying: “I think we’ll head out soon and get a cold beer.” Also breathing a sigh of relief Tuesday were fellow NATO countries. Latvian President Edgars Rinkevics said that while a lot remains to be seen, the announcement was “very positive and good.” “But I do hope that this issue is closed because it was not entirely comfortable that you have this discussion between really good friends and allies,” Rinkevics told a small group of reporters on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York. Farnoush Amiri And Jamey Keaten, The Associated Press

The new agreement builds on an existing defense deal from the 1950s that already secured U.S. military presence just by notifying the Kingdom of Denmark. Tuesday’s signature commits to the establishment of two additional U.S. bases in Greenland.
It also cements Greenland’s so-called “red lines” that secure national sovereignty of the Arctic island and its right to self-determination in a future independence from Denmark.
Only NATO members will be allowed to establish military installations on the island moving forward. The agreement does not disclose an expiry date, and demands Greenland’s commitment to the NATO alliance should it become an independent nation.
Greenlandic and Danish diplomats uttered a sigh of relief as the ink dried in the hopes that Trump, who has pushed for a U.S. takeover of Greenland in the name of national security, will hold back pressure that has made children in Greenland anxious over a potential American invasion.
On Tuesday, Trump called the process a “tremendous journey with amazing people,” referring to Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen and Danish counterpart Mette Frederiksen, who called the agreement a “milestone” in the transatlantic cooperation.
Tuesday’s agreement is the result of closed-door talks between U.S., Greenlandic and Danish diplomats. The high-level working group was established in January after an hourlong meeting in Washington that saw Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio dealing with former foreign minister of Greenland Vivian Motzfeldt and Danish foreign affairs minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen.
The past years of Trump’s takeover pressure have become a testament to Greenland’s democracy and diplomatic ability.

“Both the people of Greenland and their politicians and diplomats have shown themselves surprisingly resilient; doing an election uncompromised and insisting on a combination of sticking steadfast to principles while flexibly inviting the U.S. to engage in relation to real security problems,” said Gad.
Greenland is the world’s largest island and sits on the shortest missile path between Washington and Moscow. That gives the nation a vital geographical role in Trump’s dream of the Golden Dome project, a massive U.S. missile defense system inspired by Israel’s Iron Dome.
With climate change sea paths in the Arctic are becoming ice-free, introducing effective commercial routes and making it easier to harvest rare earth minerals and metals important for green technology, which most likely can’t be processed without China, a experts say.
Operating as a semi-autonomous country, Greenland is part of the Danish Commonwealth. Questions surrounding security and foreign affairs are officially determined Denmark, a U.S. ally, but Greenland has joined talks on such matters in recent times.
The Arctic island and its population of close to 57,000 people are determined to gain full independence from Denmark, though there’s been no agreement on when. Greenland is a part of NATO through Denmark’s membership.
After taking office in 2025, Trump declined to rule out using military force to absorb Greenland into U.S. territory, throwing NATO into its biggest existential crisis ever.
The president’s stance on using military force changed at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, this past January after Greenland officially expressed a wish to remain part of Denmark, declining any offer to become part of the U.S.
Rasmussen called the conflict a “destructive chapter in an otherwise strong transatlantic cooperation between Denmark, Greenland and the U.S.” in a social media post on Tuesday, calling a high-level working group the “strongest weapon” in Denmark’s arsenal.
Tuesday’s signed agreement must be signed off by the parliaments of Greenland and Denmark before taking effect.

Trump could've had this Greenland agreement all along | Opinion
Trump's embarrassing attacks on Greenland and Denmark have been buried under months of other, accumulating scandals – and that's exactly why he's trying to fabricate a win in New York this week.
Donald Trump, 20 months into his second term as president, and with the midterm elections looming in six weeks, is desperate to fabricate a political win as American voters sour on him and his Republican Party's control of Congress.
Trump on Sept. 18 touted a revised security agreement with two American allies, Greenland and Denmark, expected to be finalized on Sept. 22 in New York at a meeting of the United Nations General Assembly. Ending Trump's senseless war of words against these allies, this agreement would expand America's military and security presence in Greenland.
As always, Trump's announcement ran long on bluster and short on details. Here's the part he left out – everything Trump now claims as a win was available to him 20 months ago on the very first day of his second term.
It was also available for Trump during his first term, when he floated the idea of buying Greenland before threatening to take it by force in his second term after his threats were rebuffed by Greenland and Denmark.
Greenland and Denmark have existing, non-expiring security agreements and treaties that have always allowed for an American military expansion in Greenland, the world's largest island, which has significant strategic value in the Arctic Circle.
Trump's rhetoric about Greenland has been all braggadocio and bombast. That has destabilized America's relationship not just with Greenland and Denmark but across Europe and around the world.
Trump's foreign policy can be summed up in a few words – never trust him about anything.
Trump is calling an embarrassment a win
Consider how Greenland and Denmark described the deal after the U.S. president announced it.
Trump's announcement claimed that the agreement gives America "permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland, completely addressing ALL of our many U.S. concerns."
"For over 100 years, Presidents have known the strategic importance of Greenland, but NONE of them were able to do anything about it," Trump wrote in a social media post that was easily debunked by history.
Remember: American presidents oversaw the foreign policy that made Greenland and Denmark our allies for more than a century that Trump cited in his self-defeating claim.
Jens-Frederik Nielsen, Greenland's prime minister, responded to Trump's claim with a statement that said the agreement would "strengthen the security of Greenland" and "recognizes Greenland's interests."
Mette Frederiksen, Denmark's prime minister, joined in that statement to say the agreement "strengthens our common security in the Arctic" in a way that was helpful for Europe and still "recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity" of Denmark and Greenland.
Trump is trying to sell an embarrassment as a win. Greenland and Denmark sound like they just waited for our petulant president to finish his tantrum about something he wanted but could have always had if he had just asked.
Americans aren't even buying Trump's tales on Greenland
America has recognized Denmark's ties to Greenland for 109 years, in a 1917 proclamation from then-President Woodrow Wilson.
America signed a "Defense of Greenland" agreement with Denmark in 1951, when Harry Truman was president. That accord was updated in 2004, when George W. Bush was president.
Trump is not the first president to sign agreements with Greenland and Denmark. He probably won't be the last.
Greenland in 2009 became an autonomous, self-governing part of the Kingdom of Denmark, via a new law that replaced a previous home-rule policy that was instituted in 1979.
Greenland was never for sale, and Trump's threats of aggression against American allies were a national embarrassment, even for Republicans in Congress.
A 2025 poll in Greenland found that 85% of the people who lived there rejected the idea of their country becoming part of America.
Trump's Greenland aggression didn't play well in America, either. An Associated Press-NORC Poll in February found that 72% of Americans disapproved of how Trump was treating Greenland. Republicans were split down the middle in that poll, with 51% approving of how Trump treated Greenland and 48% disapproving.
There hasn't been much publicly available polling on the issue lately, as it has dropped from the news cycle as Trump's other problems pile up with his war in Iran, his trade wars with American allies, rising gas prices, increased inflation and his ever-slumping approval rating.
That's why Trump is trying to fabricate a win in New York this week. His embarrassing attacks on Greenland and Denmark have been buried under months of other, accumulating scandals. He's hoping you forgot how he tried to bully American allies but was defeated because they stood strong against him.

The arrangement, expected to be signed during the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), formally prevents non-NATO adversaries from building military installations or making sensitive investments without explicit US written approval.
US-listed stocks tied to Greenland skyrocketed on Monday (September 21) after Washington formalized a trilateral security pact with Denmark and the Arctic territory to expand American military presence.
Shares of Greenland Energy (NASDAQ:GLND) soared 159 percent,Greenland Mines (NASDAQ:GRML) spiked more than 200 percent, while Critical Metals (NASDAQ:CRML) climbed nearly 37 percent following the geopolitical announcement.
President Donald Trump disclosed the deal last week via Truth Social, stating the US will "FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the security of Greenland, and the United States of America."
He noted the agreement comes at no cost to Washington and initiates the development of a large military presence in the territory.
The agreement follows months of tension after Trump repeatedly threatened to annex the semiautonomous Danish territory, calling the acquisition "psychologically important" and declaring anything less than US ownership "unacceptable."
Danish and Greenlandic leaders emphasized that the pact maintains the island's self-determination while calming a dispute that previously prompted the Danish military to draft plans to destroy Greenland airfields in the event of an American invasion.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said in a statement that the deal "recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination."
Greenland Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen echoed the sentiment, noting the agreement "recognizes Greenland’s interests and our place in the international cooperation. It is to the benefit of us all."
Greenland Energy is a Texas-based oil and gas explorer targeting the Jameson Land Basin on the east coast, though the local government recently issued a "strong warning" to its joint venture partner over unauthorized equipment landings.
Greenland Mines controls the Skaergaard project, which holds one of the world’s largest undeveloped palladium, gold, and platinum deposits.
Meanwhile, Critical Metals is concurrently advancing the Tanbreez rare earths mine in southern Greenland while navigating a major corporate restructuring.
The company proposed an US$835 million all-stock acquisition of its Australian joint venture partner European Lithium in April 2026. The transaction will grant Critical Metals absolute control over the Tanbreez deposit by absorbing European Lithium’s 7.5 percent minority stake, eliminating the need for joint venture approvals ahead of final development decisions.
Tanbreez is considered one of the largest-known rare earths deposits globally, highly prized for heavy rare earth elements essential to electric vehicles and advanced defense systems. Western nations view the site as a key lever to break China’s near-monopoly on critical mineral processing.
Late last year, the Trump administration reportedly explored taking a direct equity stake in Critical Metals by converting a pending US$50 million Defense Production Act grant application.
